Pop Mart is a Chinese "designer toy" company — it sells collectible figurines, most of them sold in sealed "blind boxes" where the buyer does not know which variant they will get. The story it has told the market evolved in three fast stages.

Through 2021–2023 it was a China growth retailer with a stable of in-house characters (Molly, Dimoo, Skullpanda). Then one character changed everything. In 2024–2025 the "The Monsters" line, and specifically the elf-like figure **Labubu**, went from a niche collectible to a global cultural craze, pulled along by celebrity carriers and social-media virality. Revenue exploded to 13.0 billion yuan in 2024 and **37.1 billion yuan in 2025 (up about 185%)**, with net profit roughly quadrupling to about 12.5 billion yuan. **Declining — from offense to defense.** Through 2025 management spoke the language of expansion: new countries, new stores (630 stores and ~2,637 vending machines across 20 markets by year-end 2025), a flagship IP breaking records. **Medium, and freshly under pressure.** Management delivered spectacularly through the ramp, which earns credibility. But the one forward number they have put on the board — "at least 20%" revenue growth in 2026 — is already being marked down by the analysts who cover them: Morgan Stanley models about +13%, and Deutsche Bank models a roughly **−2% contraction** (May–June 2026). When the analyst community sits this far below the company's own floor within a quarter of it being set, the guidance is not yet credible for 2026. Reliability: **Medium**, trending lower.

## 5. Analyst Pressure Points

The single question management cannot fully answer: **"What is the second pillar?"** The entire re-rating debate is single-IP concentration — Labubu is ~40% of revenue, and the worry is not that Labubu is bad but that it is a *fad* whose cash flows do not annuitize. Management's answer is "we have six other IPs each over 2 billion yuan," which is true but does not resolve the concern, because none of them is a Labubu, and the group's growth math depends on the flagship. The related pressure point is **the resale market as a demand tell**: secondary prices for popular Labubu figures have collapsed — one widely-cited figure ("Luck") fell to roughly a fifth of its June peak, and some characters now trade *below* Pop Mart's own retail price (Storyboard18 / press, 2026). When the speculative premium evaporates, primary demand from flippers goes with it.

🔴 **Single-IP dependence with a visibly cooling flagship.** Labubu ~40% of revenue; China domestic online sales turning negative year over year (May 2026); US sales reported down ~45% (Bloomberg, April 2026); resale prices crashing. This is the whole bear case in one flag.

🟢 **Fortress balance sheet.** ~14.4 billion yuan net cash, no debt, Altman-Z 16.3. There is no solvency, refinancing, or forced-seller risk here — a downturn cannot kill this company, only de-rate it.

🟢 **Genuine, best-in-class unit economics.** 72% gross margin, 34% net margin, ~21% return on invested capital. Even a decelerated Pop Mart is a highly profitable franchise, and the multiple is now low-teens, not the triple-digit figure the scan reports.

🟢 **Diversification is real, if unproven as a Labubu-replacement.** Six IPs over 2 billion yuan; seventeen over 100 million; overseas now >40% of sales, with the Americas up ~748% off a small base in 2025.

## 7. Hidden Signals

The most telling shift is **from "craze" language to "platform" language.** Management is trying to re-frame the company from "the Labubu company" to "an IP-operating platform" — a durability claim designed to justify a growth multiple after the fad. The market is not buying it yet; that is exactly why the multiple compressed from a peak near 22x forward (at ~270 HKD) to ~12–13x today. A second signal: the first-ever standalone business-update call is itself the tell — companies convene those when the tape has gotten ahead of the story on the downside.

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** The business is pivoting from a single-character viral phenomenon toward an attempted multi-IP platform, at the exact moment the flagship's demand is cooling. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **is 2025's ~12.5 billion yuan of profit a peak or a base?** If Labubu is a fad, the "cheap" ~13x forward multiple is on an earnings number that is about to fall, and cheap becomes a trap. If Pop Mart is a durable IP operator whose next characters carry the load, ~13x on a net-cash, 30%-margin, still-growing global brand is a genuine fear-print.

**Moat: NARROW, and its trend is ERODING.** The durable asset is the intangible brand and the design/character-creation engine, plus a distribution flywheel (stores, vending machines, blind-box mechanics). That is a real but shallow moat — there are no switching costs and no network lock-in; a customer's loyalty is to a character, not a platform, and characters go out of fashion. The returns are high but the evidence of the last two quarters (China online sales negative, US sales down sharply, resale collapse) is that the earnings base tied to the flagship is contracting, which is the signature of an eroding — not widening — moat.

**Secular threat: manageable, not terminal.** The risk here is a **fad/retail cycle**, not a structural technology that permanently displaces the category. Collectible toys are a durable consumer category; Pop Mart's specific exposure is that its current profit is over-indexed to one hit. That is a cyclical/mean-reversion risk to *terminal earnings level*, best mapped to the retail channel-shift and hit-driven-consumer tail, but it does not zero out the terminal value the way an AI-displacement or reimbursement-cut force would. The honest read: the moat is narrow and the flagship is fading, so a low multiple on a possibly-shrinking base is a value-trap risk — but the fortress balance sheet and genuine franchise mean the downside is a de-rate and an earnings reset, not impairment.

# Pop Mart International Group (9992.HK) — A Deep Dive on the Setup

*Note on sources: no earnings-call transcript was bundled with this name. This dossier is built from the screener's financial trajectory plus current, dated public reporting — Pop Mart's 2025 annual results (released 25 March 2026), its first-quarter 2026 sales update, and May–June 2026 sell-side and press coverage. Where a claim rests on outside reporting rather than the numbers block, it is attributed. No quotes are invented.*

## 1. Narrative Arc

Pop Mart is a Chinese "designer toy" company — it sells collectible figurines, most of them sold in sealed "blind boxes" where the buyer does not know which variant they will get. The story it has told the market evolved in three fast stages.

Through 2021–2023 it was a China growth retailer with a stable of in-house characters (Molly, Dimoo, Skullpanda). Revenue was flat-to-modest — roughly 4.5 billion yuan in 2021, 4.6 billion in 2022, 6.3 billion in 2023 — and profit actually fell in 2022. This was a good-but-ordinary specialty retailer.

Then one character changed everything. In 2024–2025 the "The Monsters" line, and specifically the elf-like figure **Labubu**, went from a niche collectible to a global cultural craze, pulled along by celebrity carriers and social-media virality. Revenue exploded to 13.0 billion yuan in 2024 and **37.1 billion yuan in 2025 (up about 185%)**, with net profit roughly quadrupling to about 12.5 billion yuan. Labubu / The Monsters alone did **14.2 billion yuan in 2025, up about 366%** — it became the first designer-toy line ever to clear 10 billion yuan in a year, and it is roughly 40% of the whole company (per the 2025 annual results and CNBC/Bloomberg coverage, March 2026).

The most recent stage — the one that matters for capital today — is the **cooling**. The craze is visibly rolling over. This is the pivot the market is trying to price.

## 2. Claims vs Financials (forensic)

The headline financials are real and, unusually, they under-state rather than over-state. But the screener's *valuation* fields are broken and must be discarded before any capital decision.

| Management / screener claim | What the financials actually show | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue "up about 185%" in 2025 | Confirmed: 37.1 billion yuan vs 13.0 billion. Net profit ~12.5 billion, up ~285–309%. Gross margin 72.1%, net margin 34.4%. | Real, and exceptional. The growth and margin are genuine, not accounting-driven. |
| "Best-in-class returns and a fortress balance sheet" | Return on equity ~24%, return on invested capital ~21%, Altman-Z (a solvency score; higher is safer) 16.3, and a recomputed **net cash position of about 14.4 billion yuan** (cash 17.2 billion against 2.9 billion of debt). | Confirmed. This is a debt-free, cash-generative business. Free cash flow on a trailing-twelve-month basis is about 14.4 billion. |
| Screener: "P/FCF 151x, fair value 60, margin of safety −94%, DCF fair value 9.7" | **These fields are wrong.** At about 150 HKD the stock carries a market value near 202 billion HKD against 2025 net profit of ~12.5 billion — a trailing price-to-earnings multiple of roughly **14x, and a forward multiple near 12–13x** (stockanalysis.com, July 2026). The "151x" and single-digit fair values are a share-count or currency artifact in the scan, not reality. | Critical correction. The screener flagged this as "deep value" for the right reason (a big drawdown) but its own valuation math is unusable here. |
| "Beat 4 of 7 quarters" | Consistent with a company that repeatedly cleared its own guidance during the ramp. | Fine, but backward-looking — the ramp is what is now ending. |

The forensic point: the business quality is not in question. What is in question is the **durability of the earnings base** — whether 2025's profit is a run-rate or a peak.

## 3. Tone & Confidence Trajectory

**Declining — from offense to defense.** Through 2025 management spoke the language of expansion: new countries, new stores (630 stores and ~2,637 vending machines across 20 markets by year-end 2025), a flagship IP breaking records. By the March 2026 results briefing the tone had shifted to reassurance — management set an "at least 20% growth" target for 2026 and stressed diversification beyond Labubu, holding what press described as a first-ever business-update call to "steady market expectations" (BigGo Finance). Reaching for a floor target and a special call to calm investors is defensive body language, not offensive.

## 4. Guidance Credibility

**Medium, and freshly under pressure.** Management delivered spectacularly through the ramp, which earns credibility. But the one forward number they have put on the board — "at least 20%" revenue growth in 2026 — is already being marked down by the analysts who cover them: Morgan Stanley models about +13%, and Deutsche Bank models a roughly **−2% contraction** (May–June 2026). First-quarter 2026 revenue growth had already decelerated to about +75–80% year over year, and by May, domestic online sales fell year over year for the first time since 2024 (down ~5% versus a year earlier, ~14% versus April). When the analyst community sits this far below the company's own floor within a quarter of it being set, the guidance is not yet credible for 2026. Reliability: **Medium**, trending lower.

## 5. Analyst Pressure Points

The single question management cannot fully answer: **"What is the second pillar?"** The entire re-rating debate is single-IP concentration — Labubu is ~40% of revenue, and the worry is not that Labubu is bad but that it is a *fad* whose cash flows do not annuitize. Management's answer is "we have six other IPs each over 2 billion yuan," which is true but does not resolve the concern, because none of them is a Labubu, and the group's growth math depends on the flagship. The related pressure point is **the resale market as a demand tell**: secondary prices for popular Labubu figures have collapsed — one widely-cited figure ("Luck") fell to roughly a fifth of its June peak, and some characters now trade *below* Pop Mart's own retail price (Storyboard18 / press, 2026). When the speculative premium evaporates, primary demand from flippers goes with it.

## 6. Red Flags / Green Flags

🔴 **Single-IP dependence with a visibly cooling flagship.** Labubu ~40% of revenue; China domestic online sales turning negative year over year (May 2026); US sales reported down ~45% (Bloomberg, April 2026); resale prices crashing. This is the whole bear case in one flag.

🔴 **Growth cliff into a hard comparison.** 2025's +185% sets a brutal base; 2026 growth estimates span from +13% down to −2%, versus management's ">20%." Raw-material costs (PVC, fabric, packaging) expected up 3–5 points, shaving ~0.5 point off gross margin.

🟢 **Fortress balance sheet.** ~14.4 billion yuan net cash, no debt, Altman-Z 16.3. There is no solvency, refinancing, or forced-seller risk here — a downturn cannot kill this company, only de-rate it.

🟢 **Genuine, best-in-class unit economics.** 72% gross margin, 34% net margin, ~21% return on invested capital. Even a decelerated Pop Mart is a highly profitable franchise, and the multiple is now low-teens, not the triple-digit figure the scan reports.

🟢 **Diversification is real, if unproven as a Labubu-replacement.** Six IPs over 2 billion yuan; seventeen over 100 million; overseas now >40% of sales, with the Americas up ~748% off a small base in 2025.

## 7. Hidden Signals

The most telling shift is **from "craze" language to "platform" language.** Management is trying to re-frame the company from "the Labubu company" to "an IP-operating platform" — a durability claim designed to justify a growth multiple after the fad. The market is not buying it yet; that is exactly why the multiple compressed from a peak near 22x forward (at ~270 HKD) to ~12–13x today. A second signal: the first-ever standalone business-update call is itself the tell — companies convene those when the tape has gotten ahead of the story on the downside.

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** The business is pivoting from a single-character viral phenomenon toward an attempted multi-IP platform, at the exact moment the flagship's demand is cooling. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **is 2025's ~12.5 billion yuan of profit a peak or a base?** If Labubu is a fad, the "cheap" ~13x forward multiple is on an earnings number that is about to fall, and cheap becomes a trap. If Pop Mart is a durable IP operator whose next characters carry the load, ~13x on a net-cash, 30%-margin, still-growing global brand is a genuine fear-print.

**Moat: NARROW, and its trend is ERODING.** The durable asset is the intangible brand and the design/character-creation engine, plus a distribution flywheel (stores, vending machines, blind-box mechanics). That is a real but shallow moat — there are no switching costs and no network lock-in; a customer's loyalty is to a character, not a platform, and characters go out of fashion. The returns are high but the evidence of the last two quarters (China online sales negative, US sales down sharply, resale collapse) is that the earnings base tied to the flagship is contracting, which is the signature of an eroding — not widening — moat.

**Secular threat: manageable, not terminal.** The risk here is a **fad/retail cycle**, not a structural technology that permanently displaces the category. Collectible toys are a durable consumer category; Pop Mart's specific exposure is that its current profit is over-indexed to one hit. That is a cyclical/mean-reversion risk to *terminal earnings level*, best mapped to the retail channel-shift and hit-driven-consumer tail, but it does not zero out the terminal value the way an AI-displacement or reimbursement-cut force would. The honest read: the moat is narrow and the flagship is fading, so a low multiple on a possibly-shrinking base is a value-trap risk — but the fortress balance sheet and genuine franchise mean the downside is a de-rate and an earnings reset, not impairment.

# Forensic dossier — Pop Mart International Group (9992.HK)

*Prepared 27 July 2026. Live price used throughout: HK$165.20 (Hong Kong dollars, the 9992.HK listing on the Hong Kong exchange; source: FMP quote, 27 July 2026, +2.7% on the day, previous close HK$160.90). The company reports in Chinese yuan (RMB); the exchange rate used is HK$1 = RMB 0.8624 (FMP, 27 July 2026), so HK$165.20 equals about RMB 142.5 per share.*

**A note on sources, stated up front.** No earnings-call transcript is available for this listing — the paid data feed returns no transcripts for 9992.HK, and Hong Kong-listed companies are not required to publish them. Everything attributed to management below comes from dated press coverage of the company's results calls and business-update calls, not from a verbatim transcript, and is flagged as such. Every financial figure comes from the company's filed half-year and full-year accounts as carried by the data provider. Nothing here is invented; where I could not source something, I say so.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Pop Mart sells collectible designer toys, mostly in "blind boxes" — sealed packages where you do not know which figure you are getting until you open it. It owns the characters it sells rather than licensing them from film studios, and it sells them through roughly 600 of its own stores, thousands of vending machines it calls "roboshops", and its own apps. The economics of owning the intellectual property, manufacturing it and retailing it yourself are the whole story: a 72% gross margin in the 2025 financial year is a luxury-goods number, not a toy-company number.

The narrative has moved through three distinct phases, and the third one turned in the last four months.

**Phase one — the domestic collectibles company (2021 to 2023).** Revenue was RMB 4.49B in 2021 and RMB 4.62B in 2022, essentially flat, and operating margin collapsed to 11.6% in 2022 under China's lockdowns. This was a small, cyclical, China-only retailer with an interesting product and no proof of durability.

**Phase two — the global breakout (2024 to 2025).** Revenue went from RMB 6.30B (2023) to RMB 13.04B (2024) to RMB 36.73B (2025) — a near six-fold rise in two years. Net profit went from RMB 1.08B to RMB 3.13B to RMB 12.64B. The engine was one character line: THE MONSTERS, and within it the figure called Labubu, which became a genuine worldwide phenomenon in 2025. Management's emphasis in this phase was expansion — new countries, new stores, new intellectual property lines.

**Phase three — the cooling (2026 to date).** The tone changed at the full-year results on 25 March 2026. Founder and chief executive Wang Ning framed 2026 as a "maintenance year" — a period to service and fine-tune operations after the growth sprint (as reported in coverage of that call). That is a defensive word from a management team that had spent two years using offensive ones. The market read it the same way: the shares fell about 22.5% over the following five sessions, the sharpest such move in the company's listed life (CNBC, 25 March 2026).

Two growth drivers have been quietly introduced to fill the gap, and both are unproven: adjacencies (theme parks under the POP LAND banner, an apparel and jewellery line, building-block toys) and media (a Labubu film with Sony, announced 18 March 2026, plus a placement of Labubu at the FIFA World Cup opening ceremony — the first original Chinese character to appear at that event). Meanwhile the driver that actually produced the numbers — scarcity-driven demand for one character — is being managed *down* on purpose: the company raised Labubu output to roughly 30 million units a month in late 2025 to defeat scalpers and widen access. That decision was correct for the brand and fatal for the resale premium, which is the mechanism that made the product feel valuable.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials

| Management's claim | What the numbers say | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Growth remains strong — first-quarter 2026 revenue up 75-80% year on year, China up 100-105% (company update, 12 May 2026) | The claim is true and verified in the company's own filing. But it is a comparison against a quarter *before* Labubu went global. Deutsche Bank's channel work (note dated 8 July 2026) puts second-quarter 2026 growth at about +1.6%, against a quarter that already contained the mania | Accurate but not informative — the comparison base does the work |
| "At least 20% revenue growth" in 2026 (management target, reported repeatedly since March 2026) | Analysts covering the stock now sit at RMB 43.9B average for 2026 (+20%, 24 estimates), but the range runs from RMB 36.1B to RMB 52.3B. Deutsche Bank models RMB 35B — a 6% *decline* — which is below the entire published range | Contested. Management's floor is roughly the street's midpoint; the most rigorous bear is outside the range altogether |
| Margins are structurally high — gross margin 72.1% in 2025, expanding | True as reported. But the operating margin went 11.6% (2022) → 19.5% (2023) → 32.2% (2024) → 45.7% (2025). The last step is not scale; it is scarcity pricing and zero discounting on a fixed store base | The margin is real but the top of it is cyclical. The screener flags it at 1.7 standard deviations above the historical peak, which is the right read |
| The business converts profit to cash | It did, then it stopped. In the first half of 2025 operating cash flow was RMB 5.86B against RMB 4.57B of net profit — 1.28 times. In the second half it was RMB 5.15B against RMB 8.06B of profit — 0.64 times | This is the single most important number in the file. Cash conversion broke *before* revenue slowed |

One correction to the screener inputs, since the director will see them: the input sheet carried "trailing-twelve-month free cash flow RMB 14.37B". The filed accounts show operating cash flow of RMB 11.00B less capital spending of RMB 1.16B, so free cash flow was RMB 9.85B. The 14.37 figure appears to be the net-cash number duplicated into the cash-flow line. The same sheet carried a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 158 times; on the correct free cash flow and today's price it is about 19 times.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Declining**, and the turn is datable to March 2026.

- **Full-year 2024 results (March 2025) and the mid-2025 updates:** offensive language throughout — country launches, store openings, raised full-year ambitions. The company was in the habit of upgrading its own outlook.
- **Full-year 2025 results, 25 March 2026:** Wang Ning's "maintenance year" framing. The results themselves came in *below* what analysts expected on both lines — revenue of RMB 25.87B against RMB 27.80B expected, and earnings per share of RMB 6.91 against RMB 7.70 expected (consensus comparison series, FMP). A company that had beaten expectations for two years missed on the print that mattered most.
- **Business-update call, 13 May 2026:** the specificity shifted from demand to cost. Chief financial officer Yang Jingbing walked analysts through raw-material inflation — PVC, fabrics and packaging up 3 to 5 percentage points year on year, costing roughly half a percentage point of gross margin (as reported). This is the classic rotation: when a management team starts explaining input costs to the decimal place, it is because the demand line is no longer doing the talking.

Guidance has also become *less* specific in the direction that matters. "At least 20% growth" for a full year is a far vaguer commitment than the quarter-by-quarter country-level detail the company was volunteering a year earlier.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Medium, and falling.**

The delivery record through 2024 and the first half of 2025 was strong: the August 2025 half-year print beat on both lines (earnings per share RMB 3.74 against RMB 3.45 expected; revenue RMB 15.18B against RMB 14.93B). The screener's beat rate of four in seven is consistent with that history.

But the sequence matters more than the average, and the sequence has deteriorated: beat (August 2025) → small miss (March 2025 on earnings) → clear miss on both lines (March 2026). The most recent and largest data point is the worst one.

There is no evidence of sandbagging — the opposite, if anything. Management has consistently set public expectations at or above where the business landed, which is why the March 2026 print hurt. A team that habitually guides to the top of its range is a team whose "at least 20%" for 2026 should be treated as an aspiration rather than a floor, particularly when the most detailed independent work on the street models a decline.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Three questions recur in coverage of the calls, and management's answers have not satisfied them.

**Concentration.** Labubu and the wider THE MONSTERS line are reported at roughly 40% of revenue. Analysts have pushed repeatedly on what happens when a single character line stops growing. The answer offered is diversification into other characters and into adjacencies, which is a real answer but not yet a demonstrated one.

**The resale market.** This is the question management has the least satisfying answer to, because the company deliberately caused the outcome. When the secondary-market premium on a figure collapses from thousands of yuan to below the retail price, the "investment" component of the purchase disappears and the buyer is left paying RMB 159 for a vinyl toy. Deutsche Bank's 8 July 2026 note documents Labubu 4.0 standard editions changing hands at around RMB 50 against a RMB 159 retail price — the resale market is now pricing the product at roughly a third of what the shop charges. Management's position, reasonably, is that a healthy brand should not depend on scalpers. That is true and it is also a revenue headwind they have chosen to accept.

**The comparison wall.** Second-half 2025 revenue was RMB 22.86B, up 169%. Every analyst can do the arithmetic on what the second half of 2026 has to clear. Management has not, in any coverage I can find, given a specific second-half framework — which is itself the answer.

The topic analysts have *not* pushed hard enough on is the inventory. A 67-day increase in inventory days, in a business whose product value rests on scarcity, sitting on a 72% gross margin, is the mechanism by which a demand slowdown becomes a margin event.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **Cash conversion broke in the second half of 2025** — operating cash flow at 0.64 times net profit against 1.28 times in the first half. This preceded the demand slowdown rather than following it.
- **Inventory days from 128 to 195** over the 2025 financial year, with inventory up 259% against revenue up 182%.
- **The first year-on-year decline in Chinese online sales since 2024, in May 2026** — down 5% against a year earlier, down 14% against April, and about 25% below the average monthly level of the second half of 2025. This is the first hard evidence that the slowdown is a level shift, not a comparison artefact.
- **The full-year 2025 print missed consensus on both lines** (25 March 2026), and the shares fell about 22.5% in the following week.
- **Deliberate supply expansion to roughly 30 million Labubu units a month** (late 2025) destroyed the scarcity premium that drove primary demand.
- **No insider buying** — the screener records an insider buy ratio of zero. Management has not stepped in during a 51% decline from the high.
- **Operating margin of 45.7% in 2025** is 1.7 standard deviations above the historical peak. Earnings computed off that margin are not a normal base.

**Green flags**

- **The balance sheet is genuinely strong** — RMB 17.24B of cash and short-term investments against RMB 2.86B of total debt including capitalised leases, a current ratio of 3.5, and a solvency score (Altman-Z) of 16.7. There is no financing risk here at all.
- **Returns on capital are exceptional** — return on invested capital of 50.7% and return on equity of 69.3% on a trailing basis. Even halved, these are top-decile.
- **The business is far more than one character.** Excluding THE MONSTERS, the remaining portfolio (MOLLY, SKULLPANDA, CRYBABY, DIMOO, Hirono and others) did roughly RMB 22B of revenue in 2025 — more than the entire company earned in 2024. The single-IP framing understates the asset.
- **Capital intensity is low** — capital spending at 3.2% of revenue. Growth does not consume cash.
- **Management is choosing brand health over the print.** Killing the scalper premium and calling 2026 a maintenance year are the decisions a long-term owner makes and a quarterly-earnings manager does not.
- **Real optionality is being seeded** — the Sony film (announced 18 March 2026), the World Cup placement, the tenth-anniversary Labubu exhibition in New York (1 July 2026), theme parks and apparel. None is in the numbers yet.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The vocabulary rotated from demand to cost.** Compare the May 2026 update — basis points of gross margin lost to PVC and packaging inflation — with the country-by-country growth narrative of a year earlier. Management talks about what it can still control.

**Geography is where the story is quietly weakest.** The first-quarter 2026 detail is revealing: China revenue up 100-105%, but Europe up 60-65%, the Americas up 55-60%, and Asia-Pacific excluding China up only 25-30%. The overseas engine — the entire basis for the "global brand, not a Chinese fad" thesis — is decelerating fastest in the region that adopted Labubu first. Coverage of the Q1 update noted overseas revenue declined *quarter on quarter*.

**The store strategy changed without an announcement.** The company has shifted from opening stores rapidly to upgrading existing ones. That is prudent given a 195-day inventory and a cooling demand curve, but it also removes the mechanical growth lever that carried 2024 and 2025.

**Adjacencies arrived as a group, not as a plan.** Theme parks, bakeries, apparel, jewellery, building blocks and home appliances all entered the narrative in the same six months. A company adding six unrelated extensions at once is answering a question about the core, not executing a considered roadmap.

**A tiny share issuance on 20 July 2026** — 56,053 new shares, lifting the count to 1,331,779,203, a rise of 0.004% — is share-award mechanics and carries no signal beyond confirming the share count.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: turning.**

This is not deterioration in the sense of a business breaking. Cash generation is real, the balance sheet is fortress-grade, returns on capital are extraordinary, and capital spending is trivial. It is a business passing through the peak of an extraordinary product cycle and beginning the descent, while management redeploys attention toward extensions that may or may not work.

**The one thing the director must weigh before sizing.** Not whether Labubu fades — it is already fading, and that is documented. The question is what the *normal* earnings power of this company is once the mania is stripped out. The 2025 accounts show a 45.7% operating margin. The 2024 accounts show 32.2%. The 2023 accounts show 19.5%. If the durable margin is nearer 32% than 46%, then the earnings the market is capitalising today are roughly a third too high, and a 15-times trailing multiple is really a 22-times normalised multiple. Every valuation conclusion in this file rests on that single judgement, and no amount of further analysis of the current numbers resolves it — only the next two reporting periods will.

**Economic moat.** The moat type is intangible brand combined with a scale advantage in distribution: Pop Mart owns its characters outright (unlike Funko, which licenses other people's), employs the designers who create them, and controls roughly 600 of its own stores plus a proprietary online channel. That is a real and unusual asset. But it is **narrow**, not wide, for three reasons. First, the earnings base is concentrated: one character line is about 40% of revenue. Second, barriers to a competitor launching blind-box collectibles are low, and Chinese competitors are entering. Third, and decisively, the durability test has not been passed — Sanrio's Hello Kitty has survived fifty years and multiple cycles, which is why Sanrio trades at roughly 17 times enterprise value to operating earnings today; Labubu is two years into global fame and is already off its peak.

The trend is **eroding**. The reported returns are still rising, but that is a trailing measurement of a peak. The forward-looking evidence all points the other way: the resale premium is gone, Chinese online sales turned negative in May 2026, inventory days rose 67, and cash conversion halved. A high but *about to fall* return is an eroding moat, not a wide one.

**Secular threat: manageable.** I find no structural force — no technology substitution, no regulatory compression, no channel shift — that impairs the terminal value of an owned-character-IP business. If anything, physical collectibles and experiential retail are among the categories least exposed to software displacement. The risk here is a **product-cycle** reversion, which is severe but not terminal: a fad unwinding is not the same as a business model being obsoleted. Pop Mart at 4.8 times enterprise value to sales with net cash and 46% operating margins is not Funko, which trades at 0.63 times sales with negative returns on equity and net debt at nine times operating earnings — but Funko is the reminder of what the tail of this distribution looks like when a collectibles company has no owned intellectual property and a levered balance sheet.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither, and that is the honest answer. At HK$165.20 the stock is not actually cheap on normalised earnings — it is roughly fairly valued, having already de-rated about 51% from its 52-week high of HK$339.80. The screener's "deep value" tag is generated by dividing today's price into peak-cycle profits. There is no mispricing to harvest at this level; there may well be one 25% lower.

interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic dossier — Pop Mart International Group (9992.HK)

*Prepared 27 July 2026. Live price used throughout: HK$165.20 (Hong Kong dollars, the 9992.HK listing on the Hong Kong exchange; source: FMP quote, 27 July 2026, +2.7% on the day, previous close HK$160.90). The company reports in Chinese yuan (RMB); the exchange rate used is HK$1 = RMB 0.8624 (FMP, 27 July 2026), so HK$165.20 equals about RMB 142.5 per share.*

**A note on sources, stated up front.** No earnings-call transcript is available for this listing — the paid data feed returns no transcripts for 9992.HK, and Hong Kong-listed companies are not required to publish them. Everything attributed to management below comes from dated press coverage of the company's results calls and business-update calls, not from a verbatim transcript, and is flagged as such. Every financial figure comes from the company's filed half-year and full-year accounts as carried by the data provider. Nothing here is invented; where I could not source something, I say so.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Pop Mart sells collectible designer toys, mostly in "blind boxes" — sealed packages where you do not know which figure you are getting until you open it. It owns the characters it sells rather than licensing them from film studios, and it sells them through roughly 600 of its own stores, thousands of vending machines it calls "roboshops", and its own apps. The economics of owning the intellectual property, manufacturing it and retailing it yourself are the whole story: a 72% gross margin in the 2025 financial year is a luxury-goods number, not a toy-company number.

The narrative has moved through three distinct phases, and the third one turned in the last four months.

**Phase one — the domestic collectibles company (2021 to 2023).** Revenue was RMB 4.49B in 2021 and RMB 4.62B in 2022, essentially flat, and operating margin collapsed to 11.6% in 2022 under China's lockdowns. This was a small, cyclical, China-only retailer with an interesting product and no proof of durability.

**Phase two — the global breakout (2024 to 2025).** Revenue went from RMB 6.30B (2023) to RMB 13.04B (2024) to RMB 36.73B (2025) — a near six-fold rise in two years. Net profit went from RMB 1.08B to RMB 3.13B to RMB 12.64B. The engine was one character line: THE MONSTERS, and within it the figure called Labubu, which became a genuine worldwide phenomenon in 2025. Management's emphasis in this phase was expansion — new countries, new stores, new intellectual property lines.

**Phase three — the cooling (2026 to date).** The tone changed at the full-year results on 25 March 2026. Founder and chief executive Wang Ning framed 2026 as a "maintenance year" — a period to service and fine-tune operations after the growth sprint (as reported in coverage of that call). That is a defensive word from a management team that had spent two years using offensive ones. The market read it the same way: the shares fell about 22.5% over the following five sessions, the sharpest such move in the company's listed life (CNBC, 25 March 2026).

Two growth drivers have been quietly introduced to fill the gap, and both are unproven: adjacencies (theme parks under the POP LAND banner, an apparel and jewellery line, building-block toys) and media (a Labubu film with Sony, announced 18 March 2026, plus a placement of Labubu at the FIFA World Cup opening ceremony — the first original Chinese character to appear at that event). Meanwhile the driver that actually produced the numbers — scarcity-driven demand for one character — is being managed *down* on purpose: the company raised Labubu output to roughly 30 million units a month in late 2025 to defeat scalpers and widen access. That decision was correct for the brand and fatal for the resale premium, which is the mechanism that made the product feel valuable.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials

| Management's claim | What the numbers say | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Growth remains strong — first-quarter 2026 revenue up 75-80% year on year, China up 100-105% (company update, 12 May 2026) | The claim is true and verified in the company's own filing. But it is a comparison against a quarter *before* Labubu went global. Deutsche Bank's channel work (note dated 8 July 2026) puts second-quarter 2026 growth at about +1.6%, against a quarter that already contained the mania | Accurate but not informative — the comparison base does the work |
| "At least 20% revenue growth" in 2026 (management target, reported repeatedly since March 2026) | Analysts covering the stock now sit at RMB 43.9B average for 2026 (+20%, 24 estimates), but the range runs from RMB 36.1B to RMB 52.3B. Deutsche Bank models RMB 35B — a 6% *decline* — which is below the entire published range | Contested. Management's floor is roughly the street's midpoint; the most rigorous bear is outside the range altogether |
| Margins are structurally high — gross margin 72.1% in 2025, expanding | True as reported. But the operating margin went 11.6% (2022) → 19.5% (2023) → 32.2% (2024) → 45.7% (2025). The last step is not scale; it is scarcity pricing and zero discounting on a fixed store base | The margin is real but the top of it is cyclical. The screener flags it at 1.7 standard deviations above the historical peak, which is the right read |
| The business converts profit to cash | It did, then it stopped. In the first half of 2025 operating cash flow was RMB 5.86B against RMB 4.57B of net profit — 1.28 times. In the second half it was RMB 5.15B against RMB 8.06B of profit — 0.64 times | This is the single most important number in the file. Cash conversion broke *before* revenue slowed |

One correction to the screener inputs, since the director will see them: the input sheet carried "trailing-twelve-month free cash flow RMB 14.37B". The filed accounts show operating cash flow of RMB 11.00B less capital spending of RMB 1.16B, so free cash flow was RMB 9.85B. The 14.37 figure appears to be the net-cash number duplicated into the cash-flow line. The same sheet carried a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 158 times; on the correct free cash flow and today's price it is about 19 times.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Declining**, and the turn is datable to March 2026.

- **Full-year 2024 results (March 2025) and the mid-2025 updates:** offensive language throughout — country launches, store openings, raised full-year ambitions. The company was in the habit of upgrading its own outlook.
- **Full-year 2025 results, 25 March 2026:** Wang Ning's "maintenance year" framing. The results themselves came in *below* what analysts expected on both lines — revenue of RMB 25.87B against RMB 27.80B expected, and earnings per share of RMB 6.91 against RMB 7.70 expected (consensus comparison series, FMP). A company that had beaten expectations for two years missed on the print that mattered most.
- **Business-update call, 13 May 2026:** the specificity shifted from demand to cost. Chief financial officer Yang Jingbing walked analysts through raw-material inflation — PVC, fabrics and packaging up 3 to 5 percentage points year on year, costing roughly half a percentage point of gross margin (as reported). This is the classic rotation: when a management team starts explaining input costs to the decimal place, it is because the demand line is no longer doing the talking.

Guidance has also become *less* specific in the direction that matters. "At least 20% growth" for a full year is a far vaguer commitment than the quarter-by-quarter country-level detail the company was volunteering a year earlier.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Medium, and falling.**

The delivery record through 2024 and the first half of 2025 was strong: the August 2025 half-year print beat on both lines (earnings per share RMB 3.74 against RMB 3.45 expected; revenue RMB 15.18B against RMB 14.93B). The screener's beat rate of four in seven is consistent with that history.

But the sequence matters more than the average, and the sequence has deteriorated: beat (August 2025) → small miss (March 2025 on earnings) → clear miss on both lines (March 2026). The most recent and largest data point is the worst one.

There is no evidence of sandbagging — the opposite, if anything. Management has consistently set public expectations at or above where the business landed, which is why the March 2026 print hurt. A team that habitually guides to the top of its range is a team whose "at least 20%" for 2026 should be treated as an aspiration rather than a floor, particularly when the most detailed independent work on the street models a decline.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Three questions recur in coverage of the calls, and management's answers have not satisfied them.

**Concentration.** Labubu and the wider THE MONSTERS line are reported at roughly 40% of revenue. Analysts have pushed repeatedly on what happens when a single character line stops growing. The answer offered is diversification into other characters and into adjacencies, which is a real answer but not yet a demonstrated one.

**The resale market.** This is the question management has the least satisfying answer to, because the company deliberately caused the outcome. When the secondary-market premium on a figure collapses from thousands of yuan to below the retail price, the "investment" component of the purchase disappears and the buyer is left paying RMB 159 for a vinyl toy. Deutsche Bank's 8 July 2026 note documents Labubu 4.0 standard editions changing hands at around RMB 50 against a RMB 159 retail price — the resale market is now pricing the product at roughly a third of what the shop charges. Management's position, reasonably, is that a healthy brand should not depend on scalpers. That is true and it is also a revenue headwind they have chosen to accept.

**The comparison wall.** Second-half 2025 revenue was RMB 22.86B, up 169%. Every analyst can do the arithmetic on what the second half of 2026 has to clear. Management has not, in any coverage I can find, given a specific second-half framework — which is itself the answer.

The topic analysts have *not* pushed hard enough on is the inventory. A 67-day increase in inventory days, in a business whose product value rests on scarcity, sitting on a 72% gross margin, is the mechanism by which a demand slowdown becomes a margin event.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **Cash conversion broke in the second half of 2025** — operating cash flow at 0.64 times net profit against 1.28 times in the first half. This preceded the demand slowdown rather than following it.
- **Inventory days from 128 to 195** over the 2025 financial year, with inventory up 259% against revenue up 182%.
- **The first year-on-year decline in Chinese online sales since 2024, in May 2026** — down 5% against a year earlier, down 14% against April, and about 25% below the average monthly level of the second half of 2025. This is the first hard evidence that the slowdown is a level shift, not a comparison artefact.
- **The full-year 2025 print missed consensus on both lines** (25 March 2026), and the shares fell about 22.5% in the following week.
- **Deliberate supply expansion to roughly 30 million Labubu units a month** (late 2025) destroyed the scarcity premium that drove primary demand.
- **No insider buying** — the screener records an insider buy ratio of zero. Management has not stepped in during a 51% decline from the high.
- **Operating margin of 45.7% in 2025** is 1.7 standard deviations above the historical peak. Earnings computed off that margin are not a normal base.

**Green flags**

- **The balance sheet is genuinely strong** — RMB 17.24B of cash and short-term investments against RMB 2.86B of total debt including capitalised leases, a current ratio of 3.5, and a solvency score (Altman-Z) of 16.7. There is no financing risk here at all.
- **Returns on capital are exceptional** — return on invested capital of 50.7% and return on equity of 69.3% on a trailing basis. Even halved, these are top-decile.
- **The business is far more than one character.** Excluding THE MONSTERS, the remaining portfolio (MOLLY, SKULLPANDA, CRYBABY, DIMOO, Hirono and others) did roughly RMB 22B of revenue in 2025 — more than the entire company earned in 2024. The single-IP framing understates the asset.
- **Capital intensity is low** — capital spending at 3.2% of revenue. Growth does not consume cash.
- **Management is choosing brand health over the print.** Killing the scalper premium and calling 2026 a maintenance year are the decisions a long-term owner makes and a quarterly-earnings manager does not.
- **Real optionality is being seeded** — the Sony film (announced 18 March 2026), the World Cup placement, the tenth-anniversary Labubu exhibition in New York (1 July 2026), theme parks and apparel. None is in the numbers yet.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The vocabulary rotated from demand to cost.** Compare the May 2026 update — basis points of gross margin lost to PVC and packaging inflation — with the country-by-country growth narrative of a year earlier. Management talks about what it can still control.

**Geography is where the story is quietly weakest.** The first-quarter 2026 detail is revealing: China revenue up 100-105%, but Europe up 60-65%, the Americas up 55-60%, and Asia-Pacific excluding China up only 25-30%. The overseas engine — the entire basis for the "global brand, not a Chinese fad" thesis — is decelerating fastest in the region that adopted Labubu first. Coverage of the Q1 update noted overseas revenue declined *quarter on quarter*.

**The store strategy changed without an announcement.** The company has shifted from opening stores rapidly to upgrading existing ones. That is prudent given a 195-day inventory and a cooling demand curve, but it also removes the mechanical growth lever that carried 2024 and 2025.

**Adjacencies arrived as a group, not as a plan.** Theme parks, bakeries, apparel, jewellery, building blocks and home appliances all entered the narrative in the same six months. A company adding six unrelated extensions at once is answering a question about the core, not executing a considered roadmap.

**A tiny share issuance on 20 July 2026** — 56,053 new shares, lifting the count to 1,331,779,203, a rise of 0.004% — is share-award mechanics and carries no signal beyond confirming the share count.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: turning.**

This is not deterioration in the sense of a business breaking. Cash generation is real, the balance sheet is fortress-grade, returns on capital are extraordinary, and capital spending is trivial. It is a business passing through the peak of an extraordinary product cycle and beginning the descent, while management redeploys attention toward extensions that may or may not work.

**The one thing the director must weigh before sizing.** Not whether Labubu fades — it is already fading, and that is documented. The question is what the *normal* earnings power of this company is once the mania is stripped out. The 2025 accounts show a 45.7% operating margin. The 2024 accounts show 32.2%. The 2023 accounts show 19.5%. If the durable margin is nearer 32% than 46%, then the earnings the market is capitalising today are roughly a third too high, and a 15-times trailing multiple is really a 22-times normalised multiple. Every valuation conclusion in this file rests on that single judgement, and no amount of further analysis of the current numbers resolves it — only the next two reporting periods will.

**Economic moat.** The moat type is intangible brand combined with a scale advantage in distribution: Pop Mart owns its characters outright (unlike Funko, which licenses other people's), employs the designers who create them, and controls roughly 600 of its own stores plus a proprietary online channel. That is a real and unusual asset. But it is **narrow**, not wide, for three reasons. First, the earnings base is concentrated: one character line is about 40% of revenue. Second, barriers to a competitor launching blind-box collectibles are low, and Chinese competitors are entering. Third, and decisively, the durability test has not been passed — Sanrio's Hello Kitty has survived fifty years and multiple cycles, which is why Sanrio trades at roughly 17 times enterprise value to operating earnings today; Labubu is two years into global fame and is already off its peak.

The trend is **eroding**. The reported returns are still rising, but that is a trailing measurement of a peak. The forward-looking evidence all points the other way: the resale premium is gone, Chinese online sales turned negative in May 2026, inventory days rose 67, and cash conversion halved. A high but *about to fall* return is an eroding moat, not a wide one.

**Secular threat: manageable.** I find no structural force — no technology substitution, no regulatory compression, no channel shift — that impairs the terminal value of an owned-character-IP business. If anything, physical collectibles and experiential retail are among the categories least exposed to software displacement. The risk here is a **product-cycle** reversion, which is severe but not terminal: a fad unwinding is not the same as a business model being obsoleted. Pop Mart at 4.8 times enterprise value to sales with net cash and 46% operating margins is not Funko, which trades at 0.63 times sales with negative returns on equity and net debt at nine times operating earnings — but Funko is the reminder of what the tail of this distribution looks like when a collectibles company has no owned intellectual property and a levered balance sheet.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither, and that is the honest answer. At HK$165.20 the stock is not actually cheap on normalised earnings — it is roughly fairly valued, having already de-rated about 51% from its 52-week high of HK$339.80. The screener's "deep value" tag is generated by dividing today's price into peak-cycle profits. There is no mispricing to harvest at this level; there may well be one 25% lower.
